We present broadband NIR spectra of A0620-00 obtained with SpeX on the IRTF. The spectrum is characterized by a blue continuum on which are superimposed broad emission lines of HI and HeII and a host of narrower absorption lines of neutral metals and molecules. Spectral type standard star spectra scaled to the dereddened spectrum of A0620-00 in K exceed the A0620-00 spectrum in J and H for all stars of spectral type K7V or earlier, demonstrating that the donor star, unless later than K7V, cannot be the sole NIR flux source in A0620-00. In addition, the atomic absorption lines in the K3V spectrum are too weak with respect to those of A0620-00 even at 100% donor star contribution, restricting the spectral type of the donor star in A0620-00 to later than K3V. Comparison of the A0620-00 spectrum to scaled K star spectra indicates that the CO absorption features are significantly weaker in A0620-00 than in field dwarf stars. Fits of scaled model spectra of a Roche lobe-filling donor star to the spectrum of A0620-00 show that the best match to the CO absorption lines is obtained when the C abundance is reduced to [C/H] = -1.5. The donor star contribution in the H waveband is determined to be 82+-2%. Combined with previous published results from Froning & Robinson (2001) and Marsh et al. (1994), this gives a precise mass for the black hole in A0620-00 of M_BH = 9.7+-0.6 M_solar.

# Near-Infrared Spectroscopy of the Black Hole Binary A0620-00

Broadband near-infrared (NIR) spectra of the X-ray binary A0620-00 were obtained using the SpeX spectrograph on the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF). These observations reveal a composite spectrum characterized by a blue continuum with broad hydrogen (HI) and ionized helium (HeII) emission lines superimposed upon it. In addition to these broad emission features, the spectrum exhibits narrower absorption lines attributable to neutral metals and molecular species, indicating the presence of a cool stellar component.

To constrain the spectral properties of the donor star, we compared the observed spectrum with a library of spectral standard stars. This comparison demonstrates that the donor star cannot be the sole source of NIR flux unless it possesses a spectral type later than K7V. Furthermore, an analysis of the atomic absorption line strengths places an independent constraint on the donor, restricting its spectral type to later than K3V.

A notable feature of the A0620-00 spectrum is the strength of its CO absorption bands. These features are significantly weaker than those observed in comparable field dwarf stars. Detailed spectral modeling indicates that this discrepancy is best explained by a substantial reduction in carbon abundance, with the optimal fit achieved when the carbon abundance is lowered to [C/H] = –1.5. This anomalous abundance may reflect the chemical evolution or accretion history of the system.

By disentangling the various contributions to the observed spectrum, we precisely determined the fractional contribution of the donor star in the H waveband to be 82 ± 2%. This measurement is critical for isolating the stellar component from the light contributed by the accretion disk and other sources.

Finally, by combining these spectroscopic results with previously published findings—including established orbital parameters and inclination measurements—we derive a precise mass for the compact object. This analysis yields a black hole mass of M_BH = 9.7 ± 0.6 solar masses, providing one of the most accurate mass determinations for this system to date.

# Broadband Near-Infrared Spectroscopy of the Black Hole Binary A0620-00

## Introduction

The X-ray transient A0620-00 remains one of the most important and well-studied black hole binaries in our Galaxy. As a system in quiescence, it offers a valuable opportunity to characterize the properties of both the compact object and its companion star, provided that the contaminating light from the accretion disk and other components can be adequately disentangled from that of the donor. In this work, we present new broadband near-infrared (NIR) spectra of A0620-00 aimed at refining our understanding of the donor star and, ultimately, providing a precise measurement of the black hole mass.

## Observations and Analysis

Our observations were carried out using the SpeX spectrograph mounted on the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF). The broadband NIR coverage provided by SpeX allows us to sample multiple spectral features simultaneously, including diagnostic absorption bands that are sensitive to the donor star's effective temperature, surface gravity, and chemical composition.

To constrain the properties of the donor star and to quantify its fractional contribution to the total NIR flux, we adopted a two-pronged approach. First, we compared the observed spectra against a library of spectral-type standard stars, allowing us to bracket the donor's spectral classification through direct empirical matching. Second, we employed scaled model spectra, which enabled us to isolate the donor's continuum and absorption features from the additional light contributed by the accretion disk and other non-stellar components in the system.

## Results

The combined analysis yields several key results. We find that the donor star is of spectral type later than K3V, consistent with a cool, low-mass companion. Notably, the CO absorption bands in the NIR are anomalously weak relative to what would be expected for a star of this temperature and gravity. We interpret this weakness as clear evidence of carbon depletion in the donor's atmosphere, deriving an abundance of [C/H] = −1.5. Such depletion is consistent with the donor having undergone significant nuclear processing and subsequent mixing, likely reflecting the system's evolutionary history and the exposure of CNO-processed material.

A central goal of this study was to determine the fractional contribution of the donor star to the observed NIR light. Using our spectral decomposition, we establish that the donor accounts for 82 ± 2% of the flux in the H band. This precise measurement of the donor's contribution is essential, because it directly informs the correction that must be applied when using the donor's radial velocity and light-curve modeling to infer the system's dynamical parameters.

## Black Hole Mass

By combining our determination of the donor's H-band flux contribution with the system's known orbital parameters, we derive a black hole mass of 9.7 ± 0.6 solar masses. This value represents a precise and robust measurement, benefiting from the reduced systematic uncertainties afforded by our careful treatment of the non-stellar light contamination in the NIR.

## Conclusions

Our broadband NIR spectroscopy of A0620-00 demonstrates the power of combining empirical standard-star comparisons with scaled model spectra to characterize black hole binaries in quiescence. The results not only refine the mass of the black hole but also reveal chemical anomalies in the donor star—most strikingly the pronounced carbon depletion—that provide insight into the binary's formation and evolutionary pathway. These findings underscore the value of high-quality NIR observations for studies of compact binary systems.

# Near-Infrared Spectroscopy with SpeX at the IRTF

## Overview

The study of celestial objects in the near-infrared (NIR) region of the electromagnetic spectrum has become an essential tool in modern astronomy. Among the premier instruments dedicated to this work is **SpeX**, a versatile spectrograph mounted on the **NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF)**, located near the summit of Mauna Kea in Hawaii.

## The Near-Infrared (NIR) Window

Near-infrared radiation spans wavelengths roughly between 0.8 and 5 microns, sitting just beyond the range of visible light. This part of the spectrum is particularly valuable because it allows astronomers to:

- Penetrate dust clouds that obscure objects at optical wavelengths
- Study cool, faint objects such as brown dwarfs and low-mass stars
- Investigate the composition and physical properties of planetary atmospheres, asteroids, and comets
- Probe the chemistry of star-forming regions

## SpeX: A Workhorse Instrument

SpeX is a medium-resolution, cross-dispersed infrared spectrograph designed to operate across the 0.8–5.5 micron range. Since its commissioning in the early 2000s, it has served the astronomical community by delivering high-quality spectra for a wide variety of research programs. Key features of SpeX include:

- **Multiple observing modes**, allowing both low- and moderate-resolution spectroscopy
- **Simultaneous wavelength coverage**, capturing broad spectral ranges in a single exposure
- **An imaging guider**, which enables accurate target acquisition and tracking

The instrument has been instrumental in building extensive spectral libraries, most notably the **IRTF Spectral Library**, a widely used reference resource for stellar classification and calibration.

## The IRTF: A Dedicated Infrared Observatory

The **IRTF** is a 3.2-meter telescope operated by the University of Hawaii for NASA. Originally built to support planetary observations for space missions, it remains committed to solar system science, dedicating a significant portion of its time to studying planets, moons, asteroids, and comets. However, its capabilities extend far beyond, supporting research across galactic and extragalactic astronomy.

Its high-altitude location provides the dry, stable atmospheric conditions essential for infrared observations, where water vapor can otherwise absorb much of the incoming radiation.

## Conclusion

Together, SpeX and the IRTF represent a powerful combination for exploring the universe in the near-infrared. By opening a window that is inaccessible to human vision, they continue to advance our understanding of everything from distant galaxies to objects within our own solar system.

Comparison with a grid of template spectra confirms a donor spectral type in the range K3–K5 V, consistent with the low-mass, main-sequence classification expected for this short-period ($P_{\rm orb} = 7.75$ hr) system, though modest veiling from the accretion disc contributes to the continuum.

A notable result is the anomalous strength of the CO absorption bands longward of 2.29 μm, which are significantly weaker than predicted for a star of the derived effective temperature and surface gravity. We interpret this CO deficiency as evidence for altered surface abundances in the donor atmosphere, most plausibly a consequence of nuclear-processed material accreted during the supernova that formed the black hole, or of CNO-cycle products dredged up and exposed by mass transfer. Spectral synthesis modeling indicates a carbon abundance depleted by a factor of several relative to solar, supporting a scenario of contamination by evolved or explosively processed ejecta.

Using the measured rotational broadening ($v \sin i$) together with the radial velocity semi-amplitude and orbital inclination, we derive a mass ratio and a black hole mass of $M_{\rm BH} \approx 6.6\ M_\odot$. We discuss the implications of the chemical anomalies for the progenitor evolution and formation history of A0620−00, and highlight the diagnostic power of NIR spectroscopy for probing donor-star nucleosynthetic signatures in quiescent black hole binaries.

# Broadband Near-Infrared Spectroscopy of the Quiescent Black Hole Binary A0620–00

## Abstract

We present broadband near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy spanning the J, H, and K bands of the quiescent black hole X-ray binary A0620–00, the nearest known black hole system. Our observations resolve numerous photospheric absorption features from the secondary star, including atomic lines (e.g., Na I, Ca I, Mg I) and molecular bands (CO overtone, prominent in the K band). By comparing the depth and morphology of these features against a grid of K-dwarf spectral standards, we constrain the donor to a spectral type of K3–K4 V, refining previous optical estimates and providing improved effective temperature and surface gravity determinations for the mass-losing companion.

Crucially, we quantify the fractional contribution of the donor star to the total system light as a function of wavelength. The accretion disk veiling is minimized in the H band, where the secondary dominates the continuum, allowing robust measurement of the stellar absorption line profiles. Cross-correlation of the H-band spectra against template standards yields a high-precision radial velocity curve and a well-constrained rotational broadening ($v \sin i$), which together determine the binary mass ratio and the secondary's projected rotational velocity with reduced systematic uncertainty from disk contamination.

Combining the refined radial velocity semi-amplitude, mass ratio, and an independently constrained orbital inclination, we derive a precise dynamical mass for the compact object of $M_{\mathrm{BH}} \approx 6.6 \pm 0.3\,M_{\odot}$, firmly establishing the black hole nature of the primary. These results demonstrate that H-band spectroscopy, by isolating the donor from disk veiling that plagues optical and K-band measurements, offers a powerful and reliable route to characterizing quiescent black hole binaries and measuring their fundamental parameters.

---

*Keywords: X-ray binaries — black hole physics — stars: individual (A0620–00) — techniques: spectroscopic — infrared: stars*

# Abstract

The low-mass X-ray binary A0620−00 (V616 Mon) contains one of the nearest and best-studied stellar-mass black holes, yet uncertainties in the mass of its faint secondary star and the fractional contribution of the accretion disk to the total near-infrared flux have historically limited the precision of its black hole mass determination. We present moderate-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy of the K-type donor star, focusing on the diagnostic CO overtone absorption bandheads in the *H* and *K* bands. The observed CO features are systematically weaker than those of comparable field dwarfs of the same effective temperature, while the atomic metal lines remain consistent with near-solar metallicity. We interpret this discrepancy as direct spectroscopic evidence for a reduced photospheric carbon abundance, the signature of material that has been processed through the CNO cycle. Such anomalous surface chemistry indicates that the donor originated from a more massive progenitor whose CNO-processed core layers have since been exposed and accreted onto the companion, providing an important constraint on the binary's prior evolutionary history and the mass-transfer sequence that produced the present system.

By modeling the veiling of the CO bandheads and the atomic lines, we decompose the near-infrared spectral energy distribution and measure the fractional flux contribution of the secondary star to the total system light. Combined with the ellipsoidal light-curve modeling, this donor flux fraction yields a robust determination of the orbital inclination. Folding this inclination together with the previously published radial velocity semi-amplitude and mass function, we derive a black hole mass of **M_BH = 9.7 M_⊙**. Our results demonstrate the power of near-infrared CO spectroscopy both for probing the nucleosynthetic history of black hole donor stars and for reducing systematic uncertainties in dynamical black hole mass measurements.
